At the end of my street there is a clockmaker’s shop that has never, to my knowledge, sold a clock.

The window contains seven of them, all stopped at different times. A paper sign says BACK IN FIVE MINUTES, though the shop has been closed since I moved here eleven years ago. Occasionally someone tries the door, peers inside, and walks away checking their phone.

Last Tuesday, I saw an old woman tap on the glass. She waited, tapped again, and began to leave. Then the shop door opened.

The clockmaker was smaller than I had imagined, with a green apron and a pencil behind one ear. The woman handed him a wristwatch. He held it to his ear, nodded, and took a tiny screwdriver from his pocket.

I crossed the street slowly, hoping to see what was inside. The shelves were crowded with clocks, and at a workbench near the back, a boy was carefully sorting springs into a row of saucers.

The clockmaker returned the watch. The woman put it on, thanked him, and walked away. I reached the door just as he was closing it.

“Are you open?” I asked.

He looked down at my bare wrists. “Do you have a clock that needs fixing?”

“No. I’ve just never seen anyone in here.”

“Ah.” He glanced back at the boy, who was watching us over his shoulder. “He’s learning the trade. I thought it was time I showed him how to answer the door.”
